content: Menopause is defined as the permanent cessation of the menstrual cycle in women, occurring due to a physiological decline in estrogen hormone production, without any pathological causes. It typically occurs between the ages of 49 and 52. A woman is considered to have reached menopause after experiencing amenorrhea (absence of menstruation) for 12 consecutive months, often accompanied by menopausal symptoms. The process of menopause occurs gradually and is divided into three stages: premenopause, perimenopause, and postmenopause. Premenopause refers to the years leading up to the final menstrual period, during which reproductive hormone levels begin to decline and become erratic. Symptoms of hormone withdrawal may also appear during this stage. Perimenopause, also known as the menopause transition, encompasses the years before and after the final menstrual period, during which most women experience symptoms of hormonal fluctuations. Postmenopause is the stage following 12 months of amenorrhea, marking the end of reproductive capability. Several factors can accelerate the onset of menopause, including a family history of early menopause and cigarette smoking, which can reduce the age of menopause by approximately one year. Women who smoke are more likely to experience early menopause compared to non-smokers. It is important to differentiate menopause from other conditions that cause menstrual irregularities, such as oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, which may be associated with diseases like Sheehan's syndrome, lymphocytic hypophysitis, or hypothyroidism. Globally, menopause affects approximately 50 million women annually. Common symptoms include hot flashes, night sweats, headaches, palpitations, dyspareunia (painful intercourse), stress incontinence, urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria (painful urination), anxiety, sleep disturbances, and depression. If left untreated, menopause can increase the risk of hypertension, atherosclerosis, and hyperlipidemia. Complications such as cardiovascular disease, stroke, and osteoporosis are also common. However, with appropriate treatment and a healthy lifestyle, including smoking cessation, a balanced diet, and regular exercise, the prognosis for menopause is generally favorable. The diagnosis of menopause can be confirmed by measuring serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels, with values greater than 40 mIU/mL being diagnostic. Severe menopausal symptoms can be managed with hormone therapy (HT), non-hormonal therapies, or complementary and alternative treatments. Hormone therapy provides the most effective symptom relief but carries increased risks of uterine, ovarian, and breast cancers, as well as thromboembolism and coronary heart disease, particularly in women who initiate HT after menopause. Therefore, a thorough evaluation of symptoms and risks should be conducted by the patient and her physician before deciding on treatment. Menopause is classified into three types based on its causes: natural menopause, premature menopause, and induced menopause. Natural menopause occurs gradually and progresses through the stages of perimenopause, premenopause, and postmenopause. Premature menopause results from premature ovarian failure or medical conditions such as autoimmune diseases, type 1 diabetes, or genetic disorders like Turner syndrome. Induced menopause occurs due to surgical removal of the ovaries (bilateral oophorectomy) or as a complication of chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Pathophysiologically, natural menopause is a non-pathological process, whereas premature menopause is often associated with underlying diseases affecting the ovaries or other organs. Histopathological changes in menopause include thinning of the ovarian cortex, reduced follicle count, fibrosis and scarring of the ovarian medulla, decreased ciliated cells in the fallopian tubes, and atrophy of the vaginal mucosa. Risk factors for menopause include age, age at menarche, age at first pregnancy, number of pregnancies, use of oral contraceptives, irregular menstrual cycles, unilateral oophorectomy, body mass index, smoking, alcohol consumption, high physical activity, elevated serum lead levels, and high dietary fat intake. If untreated, menopause can lead to complications such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and stroke. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can alleviate symptoms but may increase the risk of ovarian, breast, and endometrial cancers. In the late postmenopausal stage, most symptoms resolve in the majority of women. However, untreated symptoms in high-risk women can lead to poor outcomes. The hallmark symptom of menopause is amenorrhea. Common symptoms include hot flashes, night sweats, headaches, palpitations, dyspareunia, stress incontinence, urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, anxiety, sleep disturbances, and depression. Less common symptoms include loss of concentration and self-confidence. Physical examination findings may include elevated blood pressure, hot flushes, weight gain, changes in breast size, vaginal atrophy, and thinning of external genital organs. In cases of premature menopause, signs of genetic disorders such as Turner syndrome or Fragile X syndrome may be present. Pelvic ultrasound findings in menopause include a small uterus, endometrial thickness of 5-8 mm, and small ovaries with few or no follicles. Transvaginal ultrasound is useful for evaluating postmenopausal bleeding, and endometrial biopsy is indicated in recurrent cases. Hormone therapy should be used for the shortest duration and at the lowest effective dose to minimize risks. Menopause is not preventable, but early menopause can be mitigated by lifestyle modifications such as smoking cessation, a healthy diet, and regular exercise. Secondary prevention includes HRT, monitoring for associated medical conditions, and managing postmenopausal bleeding. Early detection of these conditions is crucial for reducing morbidity, mortality, and treatment costs. Given the morbidity associated with menopause and the high cost of HRT and non-hormonal therapies, current pharmacotherapy for menopause is considered cost-effective.
